---
title: "The Short Story"
subtitle: "From the text you type to a system that uses tools and carries out work, in about ten minutes"
---

*This page is the whole course in one pass. It gives you a single mental
model and points to the lesson that develops each step. Read it first,
or read it instead of attending the talk; nothing here assumes anything
else on the site.*

## 1. You type text

Everything starts with a sentence, and a neural network cannot operate on
a sentence, only on numbers. So the text is cut into pieces called
tokens, drawn from a fixed vocabulary that was decided before training.
A token may be a whole word, a fragment of one, punctuation, or another
piece defined by the tokenizer; in many commonly used subword
tokenizers, a preceding space can affect the token. Each token is
replaced by its index in the vocabulary, a
plain integer that means nothing except "this entry", and each index
selects a row from a learned table of numbers. Your sentence has become
a short list of vectors, one per token, and that list is what the model
receives. [S-28] [S-29] `learn/how-created.qmd` traces one sentence
through these steps; `learn/tokens-context.qmd` explains why the
vocabulary is made of fragments and what follows from that.

## 2. The vectors enter a neural network

A neural network is a function with adjustable numbers inside it, called
parameters. Its smallest piece takes a list of numbers, forms a weighted
sum, applies a fixed nonlinear function, and passes the result on; many
such pieces, arranged in layers, can represent relationships that no
weighted sum alone could. Nobody wrote the parameters' values by hand.
Training adjusted them: repeatedly, a loss measured how wrong the output
was, backpropagation computed gradients of that loss, and an optimizer
used those gradients to update the trainable parameters. [S-12] [S-14]
`learn/neural-networks.qmd`
works one such piece through by hand, including one full training step.

## 3. The transformer lets each position use its context

The vector for a token starts the same wherever the token appears. What
makes the model useful is that the network updates each position's
vector using the other positions. The mechanism that does this is
self-attention: it lets each position combine information from the
positions it is permitted to use, and in the causal decoder models
emphasized here those are itself and earlier positions, never future
ones. Attention is one of two computations inside a repeating
transformer block; the other works on each position separately. A model
stacks many such blocks. [S-19] [S-22] `learn/why-transformers.qmd`
explains why transformer architectures became prevalent and what they
changed relative to recurrent sequence processing;
`learn/transformers-attention.qmd` shows the arithmetic on a three-token
example.

## 4. Out comes a score for every possible next token

After the last block, the vector at the final position is turned into one
raw score for every entry in the vocabulary. A fixed function called
softmax turns those scores into a probability distribution over the
vocabulary, and a setting called temperature controls how concentrated
that distribution is. A decoding rule then selects the next token, either
deterministically or stochastically. That token becomes part of the
context for the next generation step, and the process repeats;
implementations commonly reuse cached intermediate key and value
representations from earlier positions rather than recomputing all
earlier attention inputs from scratch. A paragraph of output is this step
repeated, one token at a time. [S-05] [S-07] [S-43]
`learn/softmax-sampling.qmd` gives the equation, an interactive, and the
reason temperature changes variety but not truth.

## 5. Why the probabilities are any good

The probabilities are worth something because of how the parameters were
set. During pretraining, the model was shown enormous amounts of text
and, at each training target, asked to predict the next token. The text
itself supplied the answer. Each time, a loss measured how little probability
the model had given the actual next token; a procedure called
backpropagation computed how the loss would change with a small change
in each parameter; and an optimizer nudged the parameters accordingly.
Repeated on a scale hard to picture, this is why the model captures
statistical structure in text: grammar, meaning, facts that recur,
conventions of argument. What it was never asked to do is check whether
the text was true. [S-05] [S-08] `learn/training.qmd` sets out the
objective, the loss, and the loop, and what they do and do not teach.

## 6. Why it behaves like an assistant

Pretraining alone does not specifically optimize a model to behave as a
conversational assistant. To shape how it answers requests, follows
instructions, and behaves within limits, its parameters are changed
further in post-training: by showing
it examples of good responses, by teaching it which of two responses
people or other models prefer, and by rewarding it for outcomes that can
be checked. These methods vary between providers and change over time,
and they all have one thing in common: they update the parameters. The
instructions a product places in front of your conversation are not
post-training; they are text in the context, and they change nothing in
the model. [S-55] [S-31] `learn/posttraining.qmd` describes the family of
methods and keeps its members straight.

## 7. Context steers a call without changing the model

Once training ends, the parameters are fixed. The request-specific
information the model conditions on is supplied through its
inference-time context: your prompt, the conversation so far, documents
that were retrieved, results returned by tools, instructions, and files
that were supplied. All of it is tokens in one finite sequence, and the
model conditions on it for this call. Decoding settings and surrounding
product logic can also affect the resulting output without changing the
parameters. If a product persists information across sessions, that
persistence is maintained outside the model and can be supplied again on
later calls; it does not by itself update model parameters. [S-31]
`learn/tokens-context.qmd`
explains what the window holds, what competes for it, and why more is
not automatically better.

## 8. Tools turn words into actions

A model call produces output. By itself it does not read a file, run a
program, search the web, or send anything. What makes those possible is
that the software around the model describes available tools in the
context, and the model can generate a structured request to use one. The
request is checked against permission rules, the action is executed, and
the result is placed back into the context for a later model step, where
it becomes evidence the model can use. The model generated the
structured request; surrounding system infrastructure, which may be the
developer's software or the provider's, executed or routed the external
action. [S-51] `learn/agents.qmd` walks through one tool call and one
whole task.

## 9. Repeat the loop, and you have an agent

Put the pieces in a loop: an objective and the current context go to the
model; the model produces a request or a response; a request is checked
and executed; the observation updates the context; the model is called
again; the loop continues, asks you, or stops. Software that runs this
loop, with tools, state, permissions, and checks around it, is the
minimal mechanism behind what this course calls an agentic system. The
word "agent" has no universally fixed boundary, and a system with a
mostly predefined path is often better called a workflow. Nothing new
appears inside the model at this stage. The same network,
the same parameters, the same next-token prediction, are being invoked
repeatedly by software that carries the state between calls. [S-56]

```
text → tokens → vectors → transformer → scores → probabilities → token
                                   ▲                              │
                                   │       appended to context    │
                                   └──────────────────────────────┘

objective + context → model step → tool request → execution → evidence
        ▲                                                         │
        └──────────── context and state updated ──────────────────┘
```

## 10. The mental model

A language model is a learned next-token predictor. Pretraining set its
parameters to capture the structure of text; post-training changed them
further so that it behaves as an assistant. Once trained, the parameters
are fixed, and everything specific to a given request reaches the model
through its context. Software around the model can give it tools and
persistent state, and can call it repeatedly, and that loop of model
step, action, and evidence is what turns a predictor into a system that
carries out work.

Four consequences follow for anyone who uses such a system. Fluency is
not evidence: the output is a plausible continuation, whether or not
anything was checked. Tool use is not automatically verification: a tool
was used only if a request was executed, and it verified only what it
was asked to verify. A passing check proves only what that check tested.
And models and tools can assist judgment, by organizing evidence, testing
alternatives, and checking mechanical claims, but on judgment-heavy
questions the system's output does not itself establish that the
conclusion is warranted; evidence, review, and human accountability
remain necessary. `learn/using-models-well.qmd` turns these into working
habits.
